ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the ethics committee of Ulm University and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
The study was approved by the ethics committee of Ulm University and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
They were recruited through the university's participant pool and received course credit or monetary compensation; no participant was excluded.
The outbound path ended when the experimenter said "stop" as participants' feet crossed the end line; participants were then turned by 180°, repositioned on the flat track, and walked back.

They were recruited through the university's participant pool and personal contacts, reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no hearing, vestibular or balance impairments, and received course credit or monetary compensation; no participant was excluded.

We measured the distance actually travelled back home: the outbound path ended when the experimenter said "stop" as participants' feet crossed the end line; participants were then turned by 180° and walked or crawled back, and the distance travelled was measured with a laser distance meter (Bosch PLR 40 C).
Participants were then led back to the start along a detour.

At the end of the two sessions that included the bridge (12° and 24°), participants were asked to draw the bridge on paper, once for each type of movement (walking and crawling), without visual access to it, and to estimate its height; they also estimated the height of the stairs.
As walking is our primary means of navigation, participants were accustomed to it, leading to more stable and accurate performance.

The outbound path ended when the experimenter said "stop" as participants' feet crossed the end line; participants were then turned by 180°, repositioned on the flat track, and walked back.

They were recruited through the university's participant pool and personal contacts, reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no hearing, vestibular or balance impairments, and received course credit or monetary compensation; no participant was excluded.

We measured the distance actually travelled back home: the outbound path ended when the experimenter said "stop" as participants' feet crossed the end line; participants were then turned by 180° and walked or crawled back, and the distance travelled was measured with a laser distance meter (Bosch PLR 40 C).
Participants were then led back to the start along a detour.

At the end of the two sessions that included the bridge (12° and 24°), participants were asked to draw the bridge on paper, once for each type of movement (walking and crawling), without visual access to it, and to estimate its height; they also estimated the height of the stairs.
As walking is our primary means of navigation, participants were accustomed to it, leading to more stable and accurate performance.

text.text: Human navigation has mostly been studied on flat ground, leaving open how elevation changes affect path integration.
In two experiments, blindfolded participants reproduced the horizontal distance home after traversing flat paths, a bridge or stairs.
Experiment 1 showed no detectable mean error after a straight flat path, but a substantial undershoot after the bridge.

In Experiment 2, bridge and stair paths produced shorter returns relative to a straight-flat baseline than did a flat path matching the bridge's profile; crawling over the bridge increased this undershoot.
Participants overestimated bridge inclination and height.
In Experiment 1, a horizontal projection based on perceived slopes descriptively covered approximately 74% of the group mean undershoot, without a detectable individual association.

In Experiment 2, an exploratory perception-behaviour correlation did not survive correction for multiple comparisons, and homing errors showed no detectable inclination effect despite different perceptual predictions.
Slope overestimation may therefore contribute to the undershoot, but its causal role remains unresolved.
One interpretation is that humans integrate vertical movements metrically using biased inputs.
The findings do not distinguish a 3D representation from projection onto a 2D representation.
Navigation studies are essential because understanding how animals, including humans, navigate in their environment helps us to understand how the brain works 1, 2 .
text.formatted: Navigation studies are essential because understanding how animals, including humans, navigate in their environment helps us to understand how the brain works <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: The discovery of brain cells that map the spatial position of an animal earned John O'Keefe, May-Britt Moser and Edvard I. Moser the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

The study of navigation has mainly focused on performance on flat, even terrain, but the last two decades have seen the emergence of studies investigating the ability to navigate on uneven terrain, that is, terrain with elevation changes such as slopes and stairs.

The main question is whether human spatial processing is isotropic, with identical properties in the horizontal and vertical dimensions, or anisotropic, with properties that differ systematically between them 3 .
text.formatted: The main question is whether human spatial processing is isotropic, with identical properties in the horizontal and vertical dimensions, or anisotropic, with properties that differ systematically between them <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: The story begins with the observation that humans prefer the horizontal plane.
Intuitively, most of us would think that we do not need a 3D representation of space, as we travel mostly in 2D.

Indeed, cities have mainly been built in valleys rather than on mountain tops, stairs are more frequent than slopes, and our morphology is not made for climbing steep slopes: even trained mountain runners cannot keep their balance on a treadmill inclined at more than about 40° 4 .
text.formatted: Indeed, cities have mainly been built in valleys rather than on mountain tops, stairs are more frequent than slopes, and our morphology is not made for climbing steep slopes: even trained mountain runners cannot keep their balance on a treadmill inclined at more than about 40° <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: Accordingly, humans perform better on even than on uneven surfaces, the so-called horizontal advantage.

Interestingly, this advantage has been reported in very different types of tasks, such as the passive reproduction of travelled distance from memory 5 , real navigation in a multilevel building 6, 7 , and spatial learning 8 .
text.formatted: Interestingly, this advantage has been reported in very different types of tasks, such as the passive reproduction of travelled distance from memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> , real navigation in a multilevel building <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> , and spatial learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> .

text.text: Although prevalent, the horizontal advantage is not systematic: some studies report a behavioural difference between the two planes without an advantage for either of them [9] [10] [11] , and one study found no behavioural difference but still suggested separate neural pathways for the two planes 12 .
text.formatted: Although prevalent, the horizontal advantage is not systematic: some studies report a behavioural difference between the two planes without an advantage for either of them <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> , and one study found no behavioural difference but still suggested separate neural pathways for the two planes <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Taken together, the literature indicates that humans' ability to navigate is influenced by the topography of the world, sometimes revealing a horizontal advantage.
These results are in line with the currently prevailing hypothesis that flying and swimming species process space in 3D, whereas walking species process it in 2D [13] [14] [15] [16] .
text.formatted: These results are in line with the currently prevailing hypothesis that flying and swimming species process space in 3D, whereas walking species process it in 2D <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> .

text.text: This hypothesis has been largely confirmed in ethology across several species: for example, rats and dogs are more accurate in the horizontal than in the vertical plane 17- 20 , whereas birds and fish perform equally well in all directions 18, 21 .
text.formatted: This hypothesis has been largely confirmed in ethology across several species: for example, rats and dogs are more accurate in the horizontal than in the vertical plane <ref type="bibr">17- 20</ref> , whereas birds and fish perform equally well in all directions <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> .

text.text: Interestingly, ants, which are terrestrial animals but can walk on vertical and upside-down surfaces, perform equally well on even and uneven terrain [22] [23] [24] [25] .
text.formatted: Interestingly, ants, which are terrestrial animals but can walk on vertical and upside-down surfaces, perform equally well on even and uneven terrain <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> .

text.text: In addition to these behavioural differences, neuroethological studies support the assumption that the locomotory style influences spatial processing.
In rodents, neural responses change depending on the dimension, horizontal vs. vertical 26, 27 .
text.formatted: In rodents, neural responses change depending on the dimension, horizontal vs. vertical <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> .

text.text: In contrast, studies on freely flying bats report 3D place cells 28 and 3D head-direction cells 29 .
text.formatted: In contrast, studies on freely flying bats report 3D place cells <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> and 3D head-direction cells <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> .

text.text: Crucially, bats differ from rats in at least one important aspect: bats fly, whereas rats walk.
Altogether, the literature suggests that spatial processing is constrained by the means living beings have for exploration.
If we follow this line of thinking, humans, as walking terrestrial animals, should have a sharp representation of 2D space and only a coarse representation of 3D space.
However, the story does not seem to stop here: recent studies challenge this hypothesis.
An fMRI study found 3D place information in the human hippocampus 30 and reported similar memory accuracy for the horizontal and the vertical planes, as did another study 31 .
text.formatted: An fMRI study found 3D place information in the human hippocampus <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> and reported similar memory accuracy for the horizontal and the vertical planes, as did another study <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> .

text.text: In rodents as well, a recent study reported head-direction cells tuned in 3D 32 .
text.formatted: In rodents as well, a recent study reported head-direction cells tuned in 3D <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> .

text.text: Although still scarce, these new results question the assumption that spatial processing is constrained only by the locomotory style.
In this context, we asked how vertical movements contribute to human path integration, the estimation of the way home from self-motion information [33] [34] [35] .
text.formatted: In this context, we asked how vertical movements contribute to human path integration, the estimation of the way home from self-motion information <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref> .

text.text: Path integration is usually modelled as the continuous summation of self-motion vectors 33, 36.
text.formatted: Path integration is usually modelled as the continuous summation of self-motion vectors <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36</ref>.

text.text: Previous human studies have examined spatial memory and learning 8, 31 , virtual navigation 5, 12, 30, 31 , multilevel buildings 6, 8, 11 and motion simulators 9, 10 .
text.formatted: Previous human studies have examined spatial memory and learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> , virtual navigation <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> , multilevel buildings <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> and motion simulators <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> .

text.text: Real movement involving elevation changes has also been studied: Zhou and colleagues tested spatial updating after stepladder descent in darkness and found preferential horizontal updating 37 .
text.formatted: Real movement involving elevation changes has also been studied: Zhou and colleagues tested spatial updating after stepladder descent in darkness and found preferential horizontal updating <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37</ref> .

text.text: Building on this work, we measured the horizontal distance reproduced on a flat return path after an outbound ascent and descent over a bridge or stairs.
A flat path matching the bridge's profile provided a control.
Our contribution therefore extends existing research on elevation and path integration to this homing task.
To investigate the nature of humans' spatial processing, we compared navigational performance on even and uneven terrain.
Specifically, we tested humans' ability to go back home (homebound) on a straight, flat path after an initial (outbound) path that was flat or inclined.
This design mirrors experiments in desert ants, which, after walking over hills, return home over the horizontally projected (ground) distance rather than the distance actually walked 22, 24, 25 .
text.formatted: This design mirrors experiments in desert ants, which, after walking over hills, return home over the horizontally projected (ground) distance rather than the distance actually walked <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> .

text.text: As in these experiments, home lay at the same height as the end of the outbound path.

Our task therefore tests whether vertical movements are taken into account accurately when computing the horizontal distance home; it does not test whether elevation itself is represented, that is, whether space is represented in 2D or in 3D.
If the isotropic hypothesis is true, the inclined terrain should be processed as accurately as the flat terrain, and participants should go home accurately in all conditions.
However, if the anisotropic hypothesis is true, the two terrains are processed differently, and performance should differ.
A horizontal advantage predicts better performance on flat surfaces.
On inclined surfaces, an overshoot is expected if the vertical component is not taken into account, as the distance travelled over inclined terrain is longer than the projected ground distance.
Additionally, we measured how participants perceived the inclined terrain, as slopes are known to be overestimated [38] [39] [40] [41] [42] .
text.formatted: Additionally, we measured how participants perceived the inclined terrain, as slopes are known to be overestimated <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref> .

text.text: In Experiment 1, participants walked back home after a flat, straight outbound path or after walking over a bridge with 24.5° slopes, and they estimated the inclination and height of the bridge.
Mean homing error did not differ significantly from zero after the flat path, whereas participants undershot the distance after the bridge.

We examined slope overestimation as a possible contributor: if perceived slopes were used to project the travelled path onto the horizontal plane, steeper perceived slopes would predict a shorter distance home.
This comparison evaluates the compatibility of the group means with a perceptual account; it does not establish that slope overestimation caused the undershoot.
Experiment 2 tested this explanation further with four manipulations.
First, we compared two inclinations, 12° and 24°: if the undershoot results from slope overestimation, it should be larger for the steeper slope.
Second, we added stairs, which involve an elevation change without an inclined surface underfoot, to test whether the undershoot is tied to the slope or to elevation per se.

Third, we added a flat control in which the profile of the bridge was laid flat on the floor, so that the outbound path had the same shape as the path over the bridge but remained in the horizontal plane.
Fourth, because it has often been claimed that the nature and properties of the inputs predict the output behaviour 43 , we compared two types of locomotion: walking vs. crawling.
text.formatted: Fourth, because it has often been claimed that the nature and properties of the inputs predict the output behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43</ref> , we compared two types of locomotion: walking vs. crawling.

text.text: We expected crawling to exaggerate the effect compared with walking, as crawling is less natural.
Twenty-seven participants (17 women, 10 men; aged 18-27 years, M = 22.0, SD = 2.3) took part after giving written informed consent.
They were recruited through the university's participant pool and received course credit or monetary compensation; no participant was excluded.
They reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no hearing, vestibular or balance impairments.
The study was approved by the ethics committee of Ulm University and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
A sensitivity analysis showed that, with 27 participants, a paired t-test had 90% power to detect within-subject effects of dz ≥ 0.65 (α = .05, two-tailed).
Participants performed a homing task on two different terrains: flat-straight vs. bridge.

They were instructed to walk an imposed distance (outbound), to stop and, once turned around, to walk back home, that is, to stop walking when they estimated that they had reached their starting position (homebound; see Figure 1).
text.formatted: They were instructed to walk an imposed distance (outbound), to stop and, once turned around, to walk back home, that is, to stop walking when they estimated that they had reached their starting position (homebound; see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: We measured the distance actually travelled back home.
The outbound path ended when the experimenter said "stop" as participants' feet crossed the end line; participants were then turned by 180°, repositioned on the flat track, and walked back.
The distance travelled was measured with a laser distance meter (Bosch PLR 40 C).

To ensure that participants relied only on the integration of their own movements (path integration 33 ), no visual, auditory or tactile cues were provided: participants wore a blindfold and soundproof headphones.
text.formatted: To ensure that participants relied only on the integration of their own movements (path integration <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> ), no visual, auditory or tactile cues were provided: participants wore a blindfold and soundproof headphones.

text.text: We built a dedicated handrail to prevent participants from veering 44 and from gaining tactile information about the distance.
text.formatted: We built a dedicated handrail to prevent participants from veering <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44</ref> and from gaining tactile information about the distance.

text.text: It consisted of two rails on which a carriage could move, like a toy train on its track.
In all conditions, participants used this handrail.
Each condition was repeated 12 times, leading to a total of 24 trials per participant.
To prevent fatigue, participants took breaks.
The order of conditions (flat-straight vs. bridge) was randomized and counterbalanced across participants.
Participants received no feedback during the experiment and saw the bridge only at the very end.
Before the homing task, we measured how participants perceived the bridge from body-based cues alone.
They were instructed to walk up the bridge blindfolded and to estimate the inclination of the slope out loud, in degrees.
Once they reached the plateau, they estimated the height of the bridge in centimetres.
Finally, on their way down, they estimated the inclination of the slope again.
The method is based on an earlier study 38 .
text.formatted: The method is based on an earlier study <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref> .

text.text: Each participant performed 7 trials, each including 3 estimates (inclination up, height, inclination down).
The flat-straight path measured 387 cm; the path over the bridge measured 420 cm (projected distance: 387 cm).
The inclination of the bridge was 24.5°, the plateau measured 51 cm, each slope 184.5 cm, and the height was 76.5 cm. 1 for the control and bridge conditions.
text.formatted: The inclination of the bridge was 24.5°, the plateau measured 51 cm, each slope 184.5 cm, and the height was 76.5 cm. <ref type="figure">1</ref> for the control and bridge conditions.

text.text: In both cases, the return distance was 387 cm.
In the control condition, participants walked on a flat surface.
In the bridge condition, the outbound path went over the bridge (24.5° slopes, 420 cm path length), while the homebound path was on flat ground.

text.text: A repeated-measures ANOVA was conducted to assess the effect of terrain type (flat-straight vs. bridge) on homing errors.
The analysis revealed a significant main effect, F(1, 26) = 96.93, p < .001, partial η² = .79 (flat-straight: 95% CI [-12, 17]; bridge: 95% CI [-110, -67]).
text.formatted: The analysis revealed a significant main effect, F(1, 26) = 96.93, p < .001, partial η² = .79 (flat-straight: 95% CI [-12, 17]; bridge: 95% CI [-110, -67]).

text.text: Participants stopped well before home in the bridge condition compared with the flat-straight condition (Figure 2): in the bridge condition, they stopped on average 89 cm before home (SE = 10.36), an undershoot of 22.9% of the 387-cm homebound distance.
text.formatted: Participants stopped well before home in the bridge condition compared with the flat-straight condition (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>): in the bridge condition, they stopped on average 89 cm before home (SE = 10.36), an undershoot of 22.9% of the 387-cm homebound distance.

text.text: This finding suggests that the inclined terrain influenced participants' homing behaviour.
Additionally, one-sample t-tests were conducted to test whether the mean homing errors differed from zero in each condition.

The bridge condition was significantly below zero, indicating a substantial undershoot (t(26) = -8.56, p < .001), whereas the flat-straight condition did not differ significantly from zero (t(26) = 0.31, p = .76).
text.formatted: The bridge condition was significantly below zero, indicating a substantial undershoot (t(26) = -8.56, p < .001), whereas the flat-straight condition did not differ significantly from zero (t(26) = 0.31, p = .76).

text.text: The nonsignificant flat-straight result indicates no detectable mean bias; it does not establish equivalence to zero.
Perception.
On average, participants largely overestimated the size of the bridge.
The height of the bridge, 76.5 cm, was perceived as 104 cm (SD = 34).
The uphill and downhill slopes of 24.5° were perceived on average as 44.0° (SD = 11.5) and 39.6° (SD = 10.3), respectively.
The overestimation factor was 1.7, which is consistent with the literature showing that perceived slant has a gain of about 1.5 relative to physical slant 41 .
text.formatted: The overestimation factor was 1.7, which is consistent with the literature showing that perceived slant has a gain of about 1.5 relative to physical slant <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> .

text.text: Projecting the bridge using each participant's perceived uphill and downhill angles predicted a mean return of 321 cm (SD = 43.5).
Participants actually returned 298 cm (SD = 53.8), against the correct 387 cm.
The observed-minus-predicted difference was -22.9 cm, 95% CI [-51.4, 5.5], t(26) = -1.66, p = .110.
This nonsignificant comparison does not establish model equivalence.
Descriptively, the predicted undershoot covered about 74% of the group mean undershoot (66 of 89 cm); this is a comparison of means, not variance explained or evidence of mediation.
Individual perceived inclination did not correlate significantly with homing errors, r = .08, p = .70.

Blue: walking back home after walking over the bridge (3D condition).
In both cases, home corresponds to the starting location that participants aimed to return to (387 cm).

text.text: Sixteen new participants (7 women, 9 men; aged 19-34 years, M = 25.1, SD = 3.7) took part after giving written informed consent; none of them had taken part in Experiment 1.

They were recruited through the university's participant pool and personal contacts, reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no hearing, vestibular or balance impairments, and received course credit or monetary compensation; no participant was excluded.
The study was approved by the ethics committee of Ulm University and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

Based on the bridge effect in Experiment 1 (dz = 1.89; paired t-test, α = .05, two-tailed), 6 participants would have provided 90% power; with 16 participants, the design had 90% power to detect within-subject effects of dz ≥ 0.87.
Experiment 2 consisted of three sessions, each lasting approximately two hours.
Participants performed a homing task similar to the one in Experiment 1 (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: Participants performed a homing task similar to the one in Experiment 1 (see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: In Experiment 2, we manipulated the inclination of the slopes (12° vs. 24°), the type of movement (walking vs. crawling), and the type of terrain (flat vs. stairs vs. bridge).

We measured the distance actually travelled back home: the outbound path ended when the experimenter said "stop" as participants' feet crossed the end line; participants were then turned by 180° and walked or crawled back, and the distance travelled was measured with a laser distance meter (Bosch PLR 40 C).
Participants were then led back to the start along a detour.

At the end of the two sessions that included the bridge (12° and 24°), participants were asked to draw the bridge on paper, once for each type of movement (walking and crawling), without visual access to it, and to estimate its height; they also estimated the height of the stairs.
We computed the perceived angles from these drawings.
As in Experiment 1, participants received no feedback and saw the bridge only at the very end of the experiment.

Each session contained four conditions, balanced for movement type (walking vs. crawling) to mitigate fatigue: the 12° bridge (walking and crawling), the 12° stairs and the 24° flat control (crawling) in one session; the corresponding 24° conditions and the 12° flat control (crawling) in another; and the straight-flat paths (walking and crawling) and the 12° and 24° flat controls (walking) in the third.
Participants performed a straight-flat path, which served as their individual baseline condition, both walking and crawling.

They also performed angled paths on flat ground corresponding to the flat control condition for 12° and 24°, as well as the stairs conditions for both inclinations (12° and 24°), and finally the bridge conditions for 12° and 24°.
All conditions were performed while walking, and all except the stairs were also performed while crawling.
This resulted in 12 conditions, each repeated 12 times, for a total of 144 trials per participant.
To prevent habituation effects and limit the time spent blindfolded, each session was divided into two blocks, with six trials per condition.
The order of sessions and conditions was randomized and counterbalanced across participants.
To add stairs and manipulate the inclination of the slopes (12° vs. 24°), the setup differed from Experiment 1.

The handrail was removed; to ensure a straight return when walking, participants pushed a trolley with fixed, straight-line wheels, and when crawling, they were aligned in the right direction and asked to move as straight as possible.
For the bridge conditions, the setup was built against a wall that participants used as a handrail, and they wore a thick glove to prevent any tactile information.
The straight-flat path (baseline condition) was 278 cm long.
For the flat control paths, the profile of the bridge was laid flat onto the floor, so that the outbound path formed the same angles (12° and 24°) in the horizontal plane.
These paths were marked with chalk on the floor of a separate room, and the experimenter turned participants by the shoulders at each turn.
For the stairs, two staircases were installed back-to-back to simulate an ascent to a plateau followed by a descent; two conditions were tested, corresponding to 12° and 24°.
For the bridge, wooden boards were fitted over the staircases to create inclined surfaces of 12° and 24°.
Each staircase was 150 cm wide and 96 cm deep, with four steps, each 24 cm deep.
The ramps of the bridges were 150 cm wide and 117 cm (12°) or 126 cm (24°) long.
The total path length over the bridge was 283 cm (12°) and 300 cm (24°).
In crawling trials (back and forth), participants moved on hands and knees while wearing protective knee pads and goalkeeper gloves to minimize discomfort and prevent tactile feedback.
In all trials, participants wore a blindfold and soundproof headphones.
For each participant and condition, homing errors were averaged over the 12 trials.

Because crawling trials started with the hands at the starting line whereas the return distance was measured behind the feet, each participant's body span was subtracted from the crawled distances; the homebound distance was 278 cm when walking.

Except for the comparison between Experiments 1 and 2 and the comparison with the homebound distances predicted from the perceived slopes, all analyses were conducted after subtracting each participant's performance in the corresponding baseline condition, the straight-flat path (walking or crawling).
Performance in these baseline conditions represents the raw estimation accuracy and accounts for individual differences.
Baseline-corrected error was defined as the participant's raw homing error in the condition minus that participant's raw homing error in the corresponding straightflat baseline.
Thus, zero after correction denotes performance equal to the baseline, rather than necessarily accurate return to the starting location.
No participants or trials were excluded, and no participant's baseline-corrected mean deviated by more than 3 SD from the condition mean.
Repeated-measures ANOVAs were Greenhouse-Geisser corrected when Mauchly's test indicated a violation of sphericity, and post hoc comparisons were Bonferroni-corrected paired t-tests.
Analyses were run in MATLAB R2024a (MathWorks).

The six Experiment 2 perception-behaviour correlations were treated as an exploratory family and Bonferroni-corrected together; unadjusted pvalues and pointwise confidence intervals are also reported where relevant.
The two follow-up perception contrasts comparing inclinations within each locomotion mode were Bonferroni-corrected as a separate family.
Nonsignificant tests were interpreted as an absence of a detected difference; no equivalence tests were performed.
To compare Experiments 1 and 2, we also analysed the raw homing errors in the baseline condition and in the 24° bridge condition, expressed as a percentage of the homebound distance.
To test for practice effects, we compared the first and second halves of the trials in each condition (the two blocks in Experiment 2).
A two-way repeated-measures ANOVA was conducted to assess the effects of condition (3D Bridge Walking, 3D Bridge Crawling, 3D Stairs Walking) and slope inclination (12° vs. 24°) on homing errors.

The analysis revealed a significant main effect of condition, F(1.42, 21.23) = 93.61, p < .001, partial η² = .86, Greenhouse-Geisser corrected, indicating that homing errors differed depending on how participants moved through the environment.

text.text: Perception.
The homing errors might relate to a biased perception of the bridge.
Indeed, participants largely overestimated the inclination of the bridge in their drawings.

Averaged over the uphill and downhill slopes, the 12° bridge was drawn at 23.8° (SD = 7.6) when walking and 26.8° (SD = 7.2) when crawling, and the 24° bridge at 40.0° (SD = 6.9) and 38.3° (SD = 6.8), respectively.
In the walking conditions, the inclinations were thus overestimated by a factor of 2.0 for 12° and 1.7 for 24°, consistent with the literature 38, 41, 42 .
text.formatted: In the walking conditions, the inclinations were thus overestimated by a factor of 2.0 for 12° and 1.7 for 24°, consistent with the literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42</ref> .

text.text: Participants also overestimated the height of the bridge by about 30 cm in all four conditions, and the height of the stairs by 20 cm (SD = 15) at 12° and 22 cm (SD = 22) at 24°.

A repeated-measures ANOVA examined movement type (walking vs. crawling) and inclination (12° vs. 24°) effects on perception errors (drawn minus real inclination, averaged over uphill and downhill slopes).
Neither main effect was significant: movement type, F(1, 15) = 0.44, p = .519, partial η² = .03; inclination, F(1, 15) = 1.75, p = .206, partial η² = .10.
The interaction did not reach significance, F(1, 15) = 4.36, p = .054, partial η² = .23.
Exploratory follow-up contrasts showed 4.2° greater overestimation at 24° than at 12° when walking, t(15) = 2.16, unadjusted p = .048, Bonferroni-adjusted p = .095 across two contrasts.
The crawling difference was -0.5°, t(15) = -0.33, unadjusted p = .747, adjusted p = 1.000.
Neither contrast survived correction, and the results do not establish different inclination effects for walking and crawling.
Link between behaviour and perception.

The exploratory correlation between baseline-corrected homing and perception errors was negative for 24° walking (r = -.53, unadjusted p = .037, pointwise 95% CI [-.81, -.04]; Figure 4), but did not survive Bonferroni correction across the six Experiment 2 perception-behaviour correlations (adjusted p = .220).

text.text: The other correlations were nonsignificant before correction: bridge angles, 12° walking, r = -.14, p = .612; 12° crawling, r = -.35, p = .184; 24° crawling, r = .01, p = .985; stair heights, 12°, r = -.25, p = .359; 24°, r = .19, p = .482.
None survived correction, providing no corrected evidence of an individual-level association.
Projection using the drawn angles predicted mean returns of 239.8 cm (SD = 19.5) after the 24° bridge and 260.3 cm (SD = 12.7) after the 12° bridge, against the correct 278 cm.
Observed raw returns were 262.1 cm (SD = 52.1) and 262.1 cm (SD = 42.0), respectively.
These distances precede baseline subtraction, as in Experiment 1: their raw errors of -15.9 cm become approximately -39.9 cm after subtracting the +24.0cm walking baseline error.
Descriptively, the 12° prediction was close to the observed group mean, whereas the 24° prediction was shorter.
The predicted undershoot approximately doubled between inclinations (18 vs. 38 cm), without a detected inclination effect in homing errors.
This comparison does not establish a causal relationship.

Comparison of Experiments 1 and 2.

Because the homebound distance differed between the experiments (387 vs. 278 cm), we computed, for each experiment, the difference in homing error between the flat condition (the baseline condition in Experiment 2) and the 24° bridge, expressed as a percentage of the homebound distance, and compared this difference between experiments.

An independentsamples t-test revealed a difference between the two experiments, t(41) = 2.08, p = .044, 95% CI [0.3, 18.0] percentage points, Cohen's d = 0.66: relative to the flat condition, participants undershot the distance home by 23.5% after walking over the bridge in Experiment 1, but by only 14.3% in Experiment 2.

In Experiment 2, the undershoot also decreased with practice in the 3D conditions: from the first to the second block, participants returned 14.6 cm further across the six 3D conditions, t(15) = 4.03, p = .001, but not across the six flat conditions (0.2 cm), t(15) = 0.08, p = .94, and this difference was significant, t(15) = 2.88, p = .011.
In Experiment 1, the undershoot did not decrease over the 12 bridge trials (trials 1-6: -86 cm; trials 7-12: -91 cm), t(26) = -0.74, p = .47.
The current study investigated the nature of humans' spatial processing by comparing navigational performance on horizontal terrain and on terrain with vertical components.
In Experiment 1, no significant mean bias was detected after a straight flat path, whereas participants undershot after walking over the bridge.
In Experiment 2, walking along the flat angled paths produced no detectable difference from the straight-flat walking baseline.
Bridge and stair paths produced shorter baseline-corrected returns, and the undershoot relative to baseline was larger when crawling over the bridge.
Slope overestimation is one possible contributor: projecting a travelled path using steeper perceived slopes predicts a shorter horizontal distance.
However, the present results do not establish that this perceptual bias caused the observed homing errors.

The behavioural anisotropy could arise from the representation of the vertical dimension, for instance the coarse, non-metric representation proposed by the bicoded map hypothesis 3, 45 , or from biased inputs used in metric integration.
text.formatted: The behavioural anisotropy could arise from the representation of the vertical dimension, for instance the coarse, non-metric representation proposed by the bicoded map hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">45</ref> , or from biased inputs used in metric integration.

text.text: Stairs constrain these accounts: participants' feet remained on horizontal treads, yet they undershot relative to baseline.
No significant difference was detected between bridge and stair walking, although this does not establish equivalence.
Thus, undershooting was not confined to an inclined surface underfoot.
Stair height was overestimated by about 20 cm, compared with about 30 cm for the bridge, but individual height overestimation was not significantly associated with stair homing errors.
A simple perceptual account is insufficient to explain the full pattern.
One interpretation is that humans take vertical movements into account metrically using biased inputs.
This would offer an alternative to a coarse, non-metric vertical representation 3, 45 and is compatible with findings of 3D spatial coding in humans and mice 30, 32 .

text.text: In Experiment 1, projecting the bridge using perceived slopes predicted approximately 74% of the group mean undershoot.
However, this descriptive agreement does not demonstrate the underlying processing mechanism, and the exploratory Experiment 2 correlation did not survive correction.
Metric integration remains one interpretation to be distinguished from alternative accounts of distance estimation and integration.

Taking slopes into account also does not require a full 3D representation: desert ants compute the ground distance of hilly paths, yet their path integrator appears to operate in the horizontal plane 23, 25 .
text.formatted: Taking slopes into account also does not require a full 3D representation: desert ants compute the ground distance of hilly paths, yet their path integrator appears to operate in the horizontal plane <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> .

text.text: With home and the outbound endpoint both at floor level, our task cannot distinguish a 3D representation from projection onto a 2D representation.
A home vector with a vertical component would be needed.
This distinction connects our findings with preferential horizontal updating after stepladder descent 37 , while our task measures return distance after both ascent and descent.
text.formatted: This distinction connects our findings with preferential horizontal updating after stepladder descent <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37</ref> , while our task measures return distance after both ascent and descent.

text.text: Slope overestimation is therefore a plausible contributor to the group mean undershoot, but whether more accurate slope perception would improve homing requires an experiment that manipulates or independently tests that perceptual input.
Several findings limit this account.
Individual perceived inclination was not significantly associated with homing errors in Experiment 1, and no Experiment 2 perceptionbehaviour correlation survived correction.
Perceived slopes predicted a larger undershoot at 24° than at 12°, without a detected inclination effect in homing.
Undershooting also occurred on stairs and increased when crawling, without a significant movement-type effect on slope judgments.
Measuring perception immediately after each trial, including an appropriate measure for stairs, would help test these relationships.
Slope overestimation is well established for both proprioceptive and visual judgments [38] [39] [40] 42 .

text.text: Its origin remains debated, but it has often been argued to have limited consequences for behaviour 38, 39, 42, 46 .

text.text: Our findings motivate testing whether it contributes to navigation errors.

This possibility may also help interpret earlier work: travelled distances are reproduced more accurately upright than when pitched backward by 30° 5 , potentially reflecting biased body-orientation estimates.
text.formatted: This possibility may also help interpret earlier work: travelled distances are reproduced more accurately upright than when pitched backward by 30° <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> , potentially reflecting biased body-orientation estimates.

text.text: Some virtual-reality studies, in contrast, detected no horizontal-vertical behavioural difference 12, 30 .

text.text: Although visual slopes can be overestimated 39 , stationary virtual-navigation tasks lack the same body-based slope signals as physical locomotion.

text.text: These comparisons suggest possible roles for perceptual inputs, but do not establish that slope overestimation causes homing errors.
We also found a clear effect of movement type on homing errors: participants undershot the distance home much more when crawling over the bridge than when walking over it.
No significant movement-type effect on perceived slope was detected, so the larger homing error was not accompanied by a demonstrated change in the slope judgments.
Because each locomotion mode was corrected by its own straightflat baseline, it cannot reflect a general miscalibration of crawled distance either.
Crawling also produced an undershoot on the flat angled paths, but a much smaller one than over the bridge, so most of the additional error is tied to crawling over the bridge.
Additionally, variability in responses was greater in the crawling condition, likely due to the unfamiliarity of this locomotion mode.
As walking is our primary means of navigation, participants were accustomed to it, leading to more stable and accurate performance.

One possible explanation for the larger errors when crawling is body orientation: when walking over the bridge, the trunk remains close to upright, whereas when crawling, it is pitched along the slope, and the horizontal-vertical anisotropy in the representation of travelled distance is body-relative 5 .
text.formatted: One possible explanation for the larger errors when crawling is body orientation: when walking over the bridge, the trunk remains close to upright, whereas when crawling, it is pitched along the slope, and the horizontal-vertical anisotropy in the representation of travelled distance is body-relative <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> .

text.text: Another possibility is that crawling over a slope takes more time and effort than walking: walked distance is estimated by combining several body-based cues 47, 48 , and path integration can be leaky 49 , so part of the outbound path might be lost, leading participants to stop earlier on their way back.
text.formatted: Another possibility is that crawling over a slope takes more time and effort than walking: walked distance is estimated by combining several body-based cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">48</ref> , and path integration can be leaky <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">49</ref> , so part of the outbound path might be lost, leading participants to stop earlier on their way back.

text.text: Interestingly, despite the differences in homing errors, no significant movement-type difference was detected in participants' perception of slope steepness; this does not establish equivalence.
We initially expected to observe this difference.
However, participants drew the bridge at the end of the session, after having crossed it both walking and crawling.
They may therefore have recognized it as the same bridge and adjusted their perception retrospectively.
Informal observations suggest that participants found crawling considerably more challenging, and many reported that the bridge felt steeper when crawling than when walking.

These reports are in line with the claim that the nature and properties of the inputs predict the output behaviour 43 , but this would need to be tested with a perception measure taken immediately after each trial.

text.text: Finally, we compared two different inclinations (12° and 24°), expecting the effects to be more pronounced at the steeper inclination of 24°.
However, no significant inclination effect on homing errors was detected.
Descriptively, the undershoot in the 3D conditions was even slightly smaller at 24° than at 12°, and only crawling on the flat angled paths led to a larger undershoot at 24°.

Perception descriptively aligned with our hypothesis in the walking conditions: steeper slopes were overestimated more in absolute terms (by about 16° for the 24° slopes vs. 12° for the 12° slopes), so that the perceived inclination predicted an undershoot twice as large at 24° (about 38 vs. 18 cm).
The walking perception contrast did not survive correction, so this descriptive pattern should not be treated as a confirmed inclination effect.
The discrepancy between perceptual predictions and behaviour remains an open question; it is the main challenge for a purely perceptual account and warrants further investigation.
The bridge-minus-flat difference in homing error was smaller in Experiment 2 than in Experiment 1 (14.3% vs.
23.5% of the homebound distance).
These percentages describe the terrain effect relative to the flat condition, rather than the absolute bridge error.

A likely reason is the much greater exposure to elevation changes in Experiment 2: 72 of its 144 trials included vertical displacement (two bridges, walked and crawled, and two staircases), compared with 12 of 24 trials in Experiment 1 (plus the seven crossings of the perception task).
In line with this, the undershoot in Experiment 2 decreased from the first to the second block in the 3D conditions, but not in the flat conditions.
This fits the idea that the horizontal advantage partly reflects our limited experience with elevation changes: with more exposure to 3D paths, participants undershot less.
Repeating the same bridge was not sufficient, however: the undershoot did not decrease over the 12 bridge trials of Experiment 1.
Other differences between the experiments may also have contributed.

In Experiment 1, participants estimated the inclination and height of the bridge before the homing task, which may have made its vertical extent salient and encouraged an explicit strategy; in Experiment 2, participants drew the bridge only after the homing trials.
The setups also differed in the height of the bridge (76.5 vs. 51 cm), the homing distance (387 vs. 278 cm) and the guidance (handrail vs. wall).

When participants finally saw the bridge, at the very end of the experiment, all of them were surprised that it was smaller than they had thought, which is consistent with their overestimation of its inclination and height.
This surprise was most pronounced in Experiment 1.
In Experiment 2, it may have been attenuated by the 12° condition and by the much longer exposure to the bridge, which gave participants time to get used to its inclination.
To conclude, elevation changes altered the horizontal distance participants reproduced on returning home.

Slope overestimation may contribute to this effect, but its causal role remains unresolved: the individual-level associations did not survive correction, and perceptual predictions did not capture the full pattern across inclinations, stairs and locomotion modes.
One interpretation is that humans integrate vertical movements metrically, but from biased inputs.
The present experiments are compatible with this interpretation without uniquely establishing it.
They also leave open whether vertical movements are integrated within a 3D representation of space or projected onto a 2D representation, as desert ants appear to do 23, 25.
